paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 7.1 – Part 7. Resolving Claims Without Trial
paragraphs.text: (1) On application, the Court may (a) order a question or an issue to be heard or tried before, at or after a trial for the purpose of (i) disposing of all or part of a claim, (ii) substantially shortening a trial, or (iii) saving expense, (b) in the order or in a subsequent order (i) define the question or issue, or (ii) in the case of a question of law, approve or modify the issue agreed by the parties, (c) stay any other application or proceeding until the question or issue has been decided, or (d) direct that different questions of fact in an action be tried by different modes. (2) If the question is a question of law, the parties may agree (a) on the question of law for the Court to decide, (b) on the remedy resulting from the Court's opinion on the question of law, or (c) on the facts or that the facts are not in issue. (3) If the Court is satisfied that its determination of a question or issue substantially disposes of a claim or makes the trial of the issue unnecessary, it may (a) strike out a claim or order a commencement document or pleading to be amended, (b) give judgment on all or part of a claim and make any order it considers necessary, (c) make a determination on a question of law, or (d) make a finding of fact. (4) Part 5, Division 2 applies to an application under this rule unless the parties otherwise agree or the Court otherwise orders.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 7.1:1 Rule 7.1 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 7.1. 1. Generally In Edmonton Flying Club v. Edmonton Regional Airports Authority, 2013 ABCA 91, 2013 CarswellAlta 294, 544 A.R. 6, 77 Alta. L.R. (5th) 389, the Court of Appeal discussed severing issues and Rule 7.1. At paragraphs 30-31, the Justices Slatter and Rowbotham said: 30 The rules of civil procedure contemplate that every action will result in only one trial, where all issues will be decided: Judicature Act, RSA 2000, c. J-2, s. 8. Rule 7.1 does permit the severance of issues, but it is exceptional. Prospects of speed, efficiency and economy from severed trials have often proved to be elusive: Gallant v Farries at paras. 13-14. An applicant who proposes to sever issues must demonstrate that it is clearly desirable to do so, and the legal test for severance is set accordingly: there must be a “real likelihood” or “good probability” of savings: Gallant v Farries at paras. 31, 48. 31 Therefore, a split trial must be one likely to achieve those aims which R. 7.1 lists: Gallant v Farries at para. 25. In other words, severing the trial must be likely to result in disposing of all or part of a claim, or substantially shortening the trial, or saving expense, or some combination thereof. As the chambers judge recognized at para. 29, if it appears that there will be a significant overlap in the evidence to be called at the two phases of the trial, that is presumptively fatal to the application: Gallant v Farries at para. 54. And at paragraph 36: “… Severance should not be ordered in a way that prevents the defendant from putting forward all its defences: Potash Corp. of Saskatchewan Mining Ltd. v. Allendale Mutual Insurance Co. (1989), 80 Sask. R. 184 at paras. 24-5, 41 C.C.L.I. 11 (CA). …” 2. Does the “Exceptional Case Test” Still Apply? In Envision Edmonton Opportunities Society v. Edmonton (City), 2011 ABQB 29, 2011 CarswellAlta 72, 507 A.R. 275, 44 Alta. L.R. (5th) 1, Justice Moen concluded that the exceptional case test is no longer applicable in Alberta. At paragraphs 49, 52–54, Moen, J. said: 49 Prior to the enactment of the New Rules, the applicable test in Alberta under Rule 221 was the “exceptional case” test: Esso Resources. Has that test now been superseded by Rule 7.1(1)(a) and the Foundational Rules under the New Rules? … 52 As I set out above, the effect of the New Rules, Rule 7.1(1)(a) and Rule 1.2, are intended to force a shift to greater willingness on the part of the courts to grant remedies that will lead to more timely and cost-effective results. 53 I find that the “exceptional case” test, as applied in Alberta, is not consistent with the New Rules. Approaching the analysis from the perspective that severance is available only in exceptional cases leads to the court focusing on finding reasons for not severing. 54 The wording of the New Rules, however, suggests that the focus should in fact be on finding reasons to sever. Rule 7.1(1)(a) sets out grounds to grant severance, rather than factors or grounds to deny severance. The suggestion is that where those grounds, or any one of them, are sufficiently strong, the court should grant severance. This reading is consistent with the purposes set out in the Foundational Rule, which stress timely and cost-effective justice. It is important to read the comments found in Gallant (Litigation Guardian of) v. Farries, 2012 ABCA 98, 2012 CarswellAlta 539, 522 A.R. 13, 60 Alta. L.R. (5th) 374, 20 C.P.C. (7th) 86, 348 D.L.R. (4th) 134 about the effect, if any, of R. 1.2 on the law interpreting R. 7.1 (see the annotation under R. 1.2). At paragraphs 8-13, 15-18, and 25-27, the Court said: 8 Counsel for the defendant suggested in oral argument that the court could decide this appeal largely on the facts and on the tests in R 7.1 of the Rules of Court. I discuss that important topic in Part F below. But that is not the approach which either the chambers judge or the plaintiff's counsel adopted. Both relied heavily on a legal suggestion in Envision Edmonton Opportunities Society v Edmonton (City), 2011 ABQB 29, 507 AR 275, 44 Alta LR (5th) 1. The facts in Envision were unusual, and the split there may have been proper. But the suggestion there was broad: to reverse all the case law on splitting trials (in paras. 14 71). The case theorized that R 1.2 of the new Rules had effected a sea change (at least on this topic), so the prior case law on splitting off issues for separate trials could no longer apply. The defendant's factum replies to that theory. 9 Since the suggestion by the plaintiff and the chambers judge could have far-ranging implications, it is better that the Court of Appeal now offer Bench and Bar some guidance on that legal topic. 10 I quote the parts of R 1.2 which are in issue here: 1.2(1) The purpose of these rules is to provide a means by which claims can be fairly and justly resolved in or by a court process in a timely and cost effective way. (2) In particular, these rules are intended to be used … (b) to facilitate the quickest means of resolving a claim at the least expense, … The Envision decision suggests that these paragraphs change the whole approach of the Rules of Court, and that therefore prior binding Alberta case law on splitting trials is repealed. 11 With respect, that suggestion is unclear. Envision's legal hypothesis would follow logically only if the aim of the previous Rules had been significantly different. Indeed that hypothesis would work only if the aim of the previous Rules was not speed and economy, but was delay and expense. I do not agree with any such notion. (It is not explicit in the Envision decision, only logically necessary.) 12 What is more, one need not speculate or extrapolate. The aim of the previous case law about splitting trials and trying issues separately, was stated there explicitly. The argument made by counsel for trying an issue separately was virtually always the same. It predicted that the split would likely save time and money, by never having to try certain issues. Of course that is the same theory which the plaintiff and the chambers judge advanced here. The courts' reply to that theory was always to see whether the split really would save time and money in that individual case. That is the same approach the defendant advocates here. 13 I will cite only a small selection of the huge body of authorities for the traditional law. That law warns that such splits are a dangerous but alluring siren, often ending by wasting everyone's time and money, not saving it. See Windsor Refrigeration Co v Branch Nominees[1961] Ch 375, 396, [1961] 1 All ER 277, 283 (CA); Elcana Acceptance v. Richmond, infra; Ratcliffe v Nakonechny, 2003 ABQB 667, 23 Alta LR (4th) 21, 44 CPC (5th) 325; Canadian Cancer Society v. Bank of Montreal (1966) 57 WWR 182, 186 (Alta CA); CMHC v. Canative Housing Corp. (1988) 90 AR 303, 304; Esso Resources v. Stearns Catalytic (1991) 114 AR 27, 29 30 (CA) (paras. 9 11); Keg River Métis Settlement v. R[1978] AUD 720 (CA). A number of these cases are binding authority. … 15 Not one of the pre 2010 cases in the slightest rejects that consistent aim of saving time and money. Quite the contrary: they expressly adopt the identical aim. They show the dangers of hopeful theorizing. They state that bitter experience shows that splits rarely achieve economy in practice; usually the result of the split (one way or the other) is to increase the time and money consumed. Savings of time and expense by severing issues have consistently proven to be elusive: LKD v JB, infra (para. 6). To adopt Dr. Johnson, splitting advocates wish hope to triumph over experience. 16 Of course splits are not forbidden, and occasionally there is good reason to think that one will save time and money. For example, sometimes a simple readily extricable preliminary issue will take little time or money, and stands a good chance of ending the suit. An expired clear limitation period, or some discrete condition precedent to suing (such as someone's permission) have been tried separately in the past. 17 In other words, all along everyone agreed on the aims of speed and economy, and all sought them. The only disagreement was on whether a particular split would advance or retard those agreed objectives. 18 Therefore, Alberta's new Rules merely recite what everyone took for granted under the prior Rules; that speed and economy are important objectives. So that statement of the tradition is no excuse for discarding all or even big parts of Alberta precedent. … 25 More specifically, general R 1.2 cannot supersede clear criteria on splitting trials in R 7.1. Its subrule (1) reads as follows: [section omitted] If read mechanically and literally, R 7.1 on splits would offer no criteria, only aims. But read in the modern purposive fashion, it means that a trial split must be one likely to achieve those aims which R 7.1 lists, not to thwart them. And those same aims are just what the pre 2010 case law on splits requires. 26 My rejection of an interpretation of R 7.1 based solely on its precise words follows a rule which the Supreme Court of Canada has adopted in upwards of 60 recent decisions. (An inventory may be found in S. Beaulac and P. A. Côté (2006) 40 Rev Jur Thémis 131.) A recent example of this rule is A G Canada v. Mowat, 2011 SCC 53, [2011] 3 SCR 471, 422 NR 248, 271 88 (paras. 33 64). Besides the exact wording of the legislation, one must also interpret it by weighing the context of its words, their history, the evils sought to be redressed, the aims of the legislation, and the scheme adopted by it to address them. Not wishing to kill trees or spill ink, I merely refer to the citations and quotations in Brick Protection Corp v. Provincial Treasurer of Alberta, 2011 ABCA 214, 510 AR 336 (paras. 31 34). 27 Paragraph 54 of the Envision decision speaks both of R 1.2 and R 7.1. If it suggests that R 7.1's own wording, apart from R 1.2, contains a radically new direction or new standard of proof, I cannot agree. I see nothing of that sort in R 7.1 itself. In Smigelski v. Smigelski, 2015 ABCA 320, Madam Justice Rowbotham said: 6 Pursuant to Rule 7.1(1)(a) the Court may order an issue to be tried before trial for the purpose of: (i) disposing of all or part of a claim; (ii) substantially shortening a trial; or (iii) saving expense. A trial should not be split unless the savings are clear or at least probable: Gallant v Farries, 2012 ABCA 98, 522 AR 13. The chambers judge found that the savings were probable here as there was a “real good chance” that the trial on the issue of the pre-nuptial agreement could save considerable time and funds for the parties in the event the husband was successful. 7 Splitting trials is the exception, not the rule. There may be situations where it is clear or probable that time and money could be saved by determining the validity and scope of a pre-nuptial agreement prior to a trial on the issue of spousal support. However, where the claims overlap, the savings are less likely. This is particularly so where the source of the payor's income for the purposes of spousal support is also one of the assets potentially available for division as matrimonial property. This Court in Lakhoo v Lakhoo, 2014 ABCA 98, leave to appeal to SCC refused, [2014] SCCA No 203, considered a similar situation. The Court allowed an appeal from a chambers judge's order bifurcating a trial where spousal support was at issue and disclosure of the payor's financial information would be required regardless of the validity of the pre-nuptial agreement. In Schlichter v. Pearce, 2022 ABQB 434, 2022 CarswellAlta 1601, Justice Richardson said: [6] The prerequisites to engaging this Rule are disjunctive, such that only one of the three needs to exist for the severance application to be considered. The question is whether there is a real likelihood that one of the prerequisites can be satisfied (Gallant v Farries, 2012 ABCA 98 at para 31). [7] The Respondent argues that once at least one of the prerequisites is found, the analysis then moves on to consider r 1.2 of the Alberta Rules of Court, in order to assess, on all the evidence available, whether severance of a claim is warranted. In arriving at this final determination, he argues that the Court must consider that the aim of the Rules is to get to the merits as quickly, efficiently, inexpensively, and fairly as possible. This approach was preferred in Envision Edmonton Opportunities Societies v Edmonton (City of), 2011 ABQB 29 at para 74 and Nowicki v Price, 2011 ABQB 133 at para 18, both decisions that immediately postdate the implementation of the current Rules in 2010. [8] I disagree with the Respondent that this second step in the analysis is a required step. This approach was rejected by the Alberta Court of Appeal in the subsequent decision of Gallant v Farries and this approach has not been adopted in any other appellate cases. [9] In Gallant v Farries, the Court of Appeal held that the provisions of r 1.2 changed nothing from the prior regime, where speed and economy were already important objectives in civil litigation: (para 18 and 24). The test remains a review of the criteria in r 7.1 and an assessment of whether a split trial is likely to achieve the aims of the section, and not to thwart them: (at para 25). Although I am entitled to consider r 1.2 in applying r 7.1, there is no required second step to the analysis: NEP Canada ULC v MEC Op LLC, 2016 ABCA 201. [10] The Appellant argues that exceptional circumstances are required to engage r 7.1. The Respondent argues that the 2010 legislative amendments to the Rules, specifically the addition of r 1.2, results in the relaxation of the previous test that required exceptional circumstances before permitting severance of a claim. [11] It is correct that the 2010 revision to the Rules removed the “exceptional circumstances” language from severance applications. However, it remains the case that splitting a trial into its component parts is the exception to the general rule that civil actions will proceed to a single trial: LKD v JB, 2012 ABCA 72 at para 6: Smigelski v Smigelski, 2015 ABCA 320 at para 7. [12] It is also correct that severance is an exception to the principle in civil procedure which contemplates that every action will result in only one trial, where all issues will be decided: Judicature Act, RSA 2000, c. J-2, s 8. Rule 7.1 is an exception to this principle: Edmonton Flying Club v Edmonton Regional Airports Authority, 2013 ABCA 91, at para 30. 3. Two Stage Procedure Remains In Manson Insulation Products Ltd. v. Crossroads C & I Distributors, 2011 ABQB 51, 2011 CarswellAlta 108, the Plaintiff (referred to as “New Manson”) brought an application for certain declarations regarding a distribution agreement between the Plaintiff and the Defendant. The application was based “on the rules for preliminary determination of issues and summary judgment based on admissions.” In the course of addressing the issues before him, Justice Poelman referred to old Rule 221, and said, “[t]his rule clearly provided for a two-stage procedure and was applied in that manner by the authorities”: paragraph 19. In respect of new rule 7.1, his Lordship said (at paragraphs 20–22): 20 In my view, the new rule also contemplates a two-stage procedure. That is clear, first, from the plain words. Rule 7.1(1) authorizes the court to order a question or issue to be heard, to define the question or issue and to give procedural directions. Rule 7.1(3) is premised upon there having been an order under rule 7.1(1) and a determination made, and speaks only to the remedies available when “the Court is satisfied that its determination … substantially disposes of a claim or makes the trial of the issue unnecessary.” Importantly, the conditions needed for the remedies in rule 7.1(3) are not necessarily required for the court to order determination of a question or issue under rule 7.1 generally. Preliminary determination of an issue might substantially shorten a trial or save expense, within the meaning of rule 7.1(1)(a), and thus merit an order that it be “heard or tried before it, at or after a trial,” while not substantially disposing of a claim or making trial unnecessary within the meaning of rule 7.1(3). Thus, rule 7.1(3) is part of the overall system that rule 7.1 provides for determination of particular questions and issues; it does not operate independently as its own procedure. 21 Second, there are reasons of economy for both the parties and the judicial system that support a two-stage procedure. The court should not be required to determine separately every question or issue in an action that the parties put before them, without first considering whether it would dispose of all or part of a claim, substantially shorten a trial or save expense. Similarly, a responding party should not be put to the expense of contesting on evidence and law the very question or issue proposed to be separately heard or tried, before having the opportunity to make submissions on whether there should be a separate determination. These considerations are consistent with the purpose and intention of the new rules as set out in rule 1.2, which emphasize resolution of claims in a timely and cost-effective way and discourage applications that do not achieve that purpose. Preserving a two-stage procedure enables the court to ensure that separate determination of issues will occur only in proper cases. 22 New Manson has not applied for an order under rule 7.1(1). Rather it has applied directly under rule 7.1(3), which assumes that the court has found that there should be a preliminary determination of the matters on which a declaration is sought. For this reason alone, New Manson's application must fail. Justice Poelman then considered an application under R. 7.1(1), and said (at paragraph 23): 23 If New Manson's application were to be treated as though it were under rule 7.1(1), it would be necessary to consider whether the proposed determination of the requested declaration would dispose of all or part of a claim, substantially shorten a trial or save expense. While there are changes from the former rule 221 to the new rule 7.1, some of the authorities considering the former rule remain instructive. In particular, I note the Court of Appeal's warnings about “piecemeal” determination of preliminary issues in Esso Resources Canada Limited v. Stearns Catalytic Ltd. 4. Severance vs. Summary Judgment In L. (P.) v. Alberta, 2011 ABQB 771, 2011 CarswellAlta 2262, Graesser, J. said, at paragraphs 53-54, and 56–60: 53 The fact that severance might have been sought does not answer the question, however. Severance seeks the court's direction that an issue be hived off the remaining claims and determined before other claims proceed. Severance suggests that the issue to be tried will still be subject to disclosure of information procedures (record production and questioning), expert witness report exchanges and likely an alternative dispute resolution process (or waiver) under R. 4.16. 54 Summary judgment does not require that there have been any record production or questioning, and the ADR requirement is not applicable to summary judgment, as it seeks to avoid a trial. … 56 Severance contemplates an order for an issue to be heard or tried “disposing of all or part of a claim” (R. 7.1(1)(a)(i)). This wording is substantially the same as R. 7.3(1)(c). 57 In my view, these rules must be read together, as offering the parties choices of a course of action. If a party believes that resolution of one issue amongst many might “dispose of all or part of a claim, substantially shorten the trial, or save expense”, but the party still requires record production, questioning, expert report production and a trial, severance may be the appropriate route to follow. 58 If the party believes that an issue can be determined in a summary way (i.e. without trial), because there have been admissions of fact or the only evidence necessary is in the form of authentic records, summary judgment may be the appropriate route to follow. 59 The foundational rules emphasize the objectives of fairness, justice, efficiency, economy and proportionality. Having regard to the high financial and emotional cost of litigation and the time usually taken by the full litigation process, parties should be encouraged to pursue strategies which may shorten the proceedings. That is one of the reasons mandatory ADR has been introduced. 60 I note that the cases on severance which have been decided since the new rules came into effect in November, 2010, (Envision, Nowicki and Ponich) appear to be lessening the barriers to severance which existed under the old rules. In particular, I refer to Veit J.'s comments in Ponich, at para. 9: • New Rule 7.1 is considerably broader in scope than the Rules it replaces and explicitly authorizes the granting of orders designed either to dispose of part of a claim or to save expense; • the new foundational rules in the Rules of Court require a court to consider how trials can be heard as expeditiously as possible … 5. Must Facts Alleged Be Proved? Generally, the application is brought by a party who is of the view that, even on the facts as alleged by the other side, a decisive point of law will be decided in favour of the applicant. Therefore, one must take the facts as alleged by the respondent. The first question is as to what materials my decision should be based on. The answer to that question is that, in this case, the allegations of fact alleged in the pleadings of the plaintiff are to be taken as true and the allegations of fact in the pleadings of the defendant are not to be regarded. It was so held in the Bank of Ottawa v. Township of Roxborough et al. (1909), 18 O.L.R. 511, a decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal, in which decision Moss, C.J.O., at pp. 518-9, said the following: For the purposes of the argument as to want of jurisdiction, the allegations of the statement of defence ought not to be regarded. Unless this were so, a defendant might support his point of law by putting upon record statements which were untrue in fact and which he would utterly fail to support by evidence at a trial. No doubt the parties might admit all the essential facts that could be proved on both sides and thus reduce the matter to a pure point of law, but that is not this case. Looking, therefore, at the allegations of the statement of claim, which the plaintiffs undertake to prove, if permitted, and assuming, as for the purposes of the discussion of the point of law it should be, that they are true, I am unable to say at present that the High Court has not jurisdiction to entertain the action. That case was followed in Green v. Spencer et al., [1939] O.W.N. 47 … in which case Kelly, J., at p. 48, stated the law succinctly as follows: It has been laid down in Bank of Ottawa v. Township of Roxborough (1909), 18 O.L.R. 511, that in considering the point of law allegations of fact in the pleadings of the party raising the point of law cannot be regarded, and that all allegations of fact alleged in the opposite pleading are to be taken as true. The point of law must be one arising out of facts clearly admitted in the pleadings. … It would appear therefore that the issue should be decided on the assumption that the facts set out in the plaintiff's pleadings are true … It is clear, therefore, that the point of law raised must be clear and the decision not contingent on the resolution of any dispute as to facts … … that which is raised in a reply should be considered. Therefore, if as a result of a reply a factual issue necessary for deciding the point of law remains unresolved, the point of law cannot be decided on a motion under Rule 124. [Alberta, R. 220]. Piuti v. Toronto (Board of Education) (1974), 6 O.R. (2d) 172 at 173 to 178 (H.C.). It can be concluded that if the facts as pleaded by the respondent are not clear, then a R. 7.1 application is inappropriate. A preliminary question of law under Rule 220 of the Supreme Court Rules must be decided by assuming for the purpose of the motion only, that all facts alleged in the material before the court are true …McCarthy v. Calgary Roman Catholic Separate School District No. 1 (1979), 26 A.R. 1 at 7 (T.D.). Note that the court does not rely on the allegations of fact contained in the applicant's pleadings. Plaintiff sued three defendants for falsely imprisoning him in the Ontario Hospital at London. One of the defendants moved for leave to set down for hearing before trial the following point of law raised in the defence, “…. that plaintiff's action is barred on the ground that he has brought this action without first obtaining the consent of the Attorney-General of Ontario as required by the Mental Hospitals Act, R.S.O. 1937, c. 392, s. 10.” Kelly J. said that no point of law arose on the pleadings within the meaning of Rule 122, for nowhere in plaintiff's pleadings did it appear that consent of the Attorney-General was not obtained, and defendant could not have a point of law determined under the Rule upon allegations of fact in his own pleadings. Green v. Spencer, [1939] 1 D.L.R. 777 (Ont. S.C.), per Kelly J. 6. Disputed Facts The courts have often held that a preliminary question of law, or similar split of the case, must not be used where the result can depend upon the facts. Armstrong v. McLaughlin Estate (1995), 178 A.R. 125 (C.A.), at 126, per Côté J.A. 7. Effect of R. 7.1 Order With all due respect to the learned chambers judge, he misconceived the effect of a decision on a point of law under R. 220. He erred in concluding that it was open to the plaintiff to adduce further evidence at trial on the question decided by Dechene J., upon which the trial judge could make a different disposition of the point of law. That question decided by Dechene J., and the Court of Appeal was res judicata, even though these decisions may not have been final determination of all the issues in the action. The hearing of a point of law under R. 220 is surely not a mere procedure for testing the waters for prospective litigation with a view to guiding the parties into secure legal positions, for that would clearly be an abuse of process. The courts do not decide hypothetical questions. Such a hearing is an alternative route for disposition of a point of law for the purpose of the trial. The words in R. 220 “otherwise it shall be disposed of at trial” contemplate that such a disposition shall be made at the hearing. The facts admitted on the submission of a point of law for determination under R. 220 are deemed to be all of the facts relevant to the point of law as if they had been established in evidence on that issue at the trial had the issue proceeded to trial. The parties are bound by those facts on that point to the same extent that they would have been had the facts been found by the trial judge on evidence adduced before him. A judicial determination of a point of law on the admitted facts has the same binding effect that it would have had if made at the conclusion of the trial. Once entered the decision operates as an estoppel by res judicata if the same point is sought to be relitigated or reargued by the same parties, whether in the same action or another. The learned chambers judge was of the opinion that the decision of Dechene J. and that of the Court of Appeal affirming it did not create estoppel by res judicata because it was not the final judgment in the action. But it is not only the final judgment in an action which will be res judicata. Estoppel by res judicata is created by any judicial decision which “finally” determines the rights of the parties inter se. Guarantee Trust Co. v. Bailey (1987), 52 Alta. L.R. (2d) 289 at 295-96 (C.A.). 8. Are Questions on Admissibility of Evidence Appropriate? While this was neither raised nor argued by the parties in the appeal, I should like to add that, in my opinion, the question placed before Mr. Justice Girgulis being one of admissibility of evidence should normally have been dealt with by the trial judge. I doubt that it was the proper subject for determination on a point of law under R. 220 unless by the trial judge himself. This judgment should not be read as endorsing the procedure followed here, the point being left open for future determination. Guarantee Trust Co. v. Bailey, supra, at 303. 9. Granting Security under Rule I see nothing in the rules under consideration that would make it improper for a chambers Judge to exact some form of security as a condition of granting the order requested here. Perhaps as a general rule there would be no need for such a requirement. It would appear that the learned chambers judge had some anxiety that should the issue of liability become involved in a series of appeals resulting in ultimate delay, the appellant's claim for damages on the counterclaim if finally held to be a valid one, should be protected at least to some extent. I can see nothing wrong in such an approach. I can see nothing wrong either in the requiring of a bond of indemnity as a condition to the granting of the relief sought under the special circumstances of the present case. Karlsen Shipping Co. v. Sefel J. & Associates Ltd. (1978), 9 A.R. 341 (C.A.), at 347-48, per Morrow J. 10. Leave Required One must first seek leave to have a matter heard. Generally, all substantive issues in a defended action should be decided at trial. There are various exceptions to that. One of them is found in Rule 221. In my view, Rule 221 involves a two step procedure identical to Rule 220. In Town of Spruce Grove v. Yellowhead Regional Library Board (1983), 44 A.R. 408, Laycraft, J.A., states at p. 50: Rule 220 of the Rules of Court enables the parties to pose a preliminary point of law for determination by the court only ‘with leave of the court’. Application is made in chambers for leave and, if it is granted, the questions are formulated. That procedure does not appear to have been followed in this case. Rather the parties simply appeared in Queen's Bench chambers by agreement and proceeded to argue the three questions they had devised. The chambers judge apparently assumed an order had been made giving leave and proceeded directly to the questions. Had the prescribed procedure been followed, leave might well have been refused. Not only do the points of law raised go beyond the pleadings, but there appears to be no compelling reason not to bring all parts of the case forward at the same time. The evidence in this case will surely not take more than few minutes to adduce. All issues could then have been resolved at once rather than in the present fragmented fashion. Although the terminology of the two rules is somewhat different I believe that both involve a preliminary screening process by the Court to determine whether it is appropriate that some issue be tried other than at trial. I do not agree that Rule 221 allows a party to make an application for a determination of an issue without more. Rule 221 says the Court may order any issue “to be tried before, at or after the trial”. Without such an order a party cannot just jump in and try to have the merits of an issue adjudicated on before trial. Skagos v. Emery Jamieson (1986), 72 A.R. 231 ((Master)), at 239, per Master Funduk. 11. Same Judge Need Not Hear Severed Trials In Jen-Col Construction Ltd. v. Parkland (County) No. 31 (2000), 269 A.R. 352 (Q.B.), the liability issue had been severed from the quantum of damage issue. Veit, J. was asked whether the same judge had to hear both trials. At p. 354, her Ladyship said: The liability trial judge is not seized of the damages issue. The court has discretion to decide whether it is seized of the completion of the trial. In making such a decision, the court should have regard to at least the following factors: efficiency, utilization of court resources, and potential prejudice. In this case, there was no important evidence led on the liability trial that dealt in any way with the issue of damages. Nor were there any real findings on credibility that would bind any other judge hearing the liability trial. There would be no prejudice either way to either of the parties. Therefore, on the facts of this case, the Chief Justice will make the assignment of the judge who will hear the remaining issues. 12. Questions of Mixed Law and Fact However, I respectfully agree with the decision of Cooke J., on a similar application by a hospital in Jaffer v. Schultze (February 5, 1991), Edmonton 8803 14161 (Alta. Q.B.), in which he concluded that the use of the related R. 221 for the determination of preliminary points is not appropriate where the issue is one of mixed fact and law, in denying the application. Brown (Next Friend of) v. University of Alberta Hospital (1995), 31 Alta. L.R. (3d) 260 (Q.B.), at 264, per Bielby J. 13. Applications Concerning Limitation Dates If there are no disputes of fact limitation defences are probably susceptible to a pre-trial adjudication. If a limitation defence is successful that concludes the action. A successful limitation defence obviates the necessity to deal with the merits of the claim in any fashion. Skagos v. Emery Jamieson (1986), 72 A.R. 231 (Master), at 239, per Master Funduk. 14. Limitations of Rule We agree that rule 221 does not authorize a trial judge to send out, as it were, a part of the trial in a case where the issues sent out are inextricably bound up with the issues raised in the pleadings that he must finally determine, and that involve questions of fact and, probably, questions of credibility. Jackson v. Trimac Industries Ltd. (1991), 116 A.R. 71 at 75 (C.A.). 15. Issue not defined by pleadings In Snowbird Rentals Ltd. v. B.T.U. Panels Ltd. (1987), 79 A.R. 120 (Master), the court invoked R. 222 to order the preparation of pleadings for an action transferred to the Court of Queen's Bench from Provincial Court. In quoting Canadian Overnite Courier (1983) Ltd. v. Jasper Printing Group Ltd. (January 15, 1985), Doc. 8403 25681 (Q.B.), Master Funduk said at p. 122: In this Court pleadings define the issues and determine the scope of examinations for discovery. In addition, any judgment given must be based on the issues placed before the Court by the pleadings: Creditel of Canada v. Terrace Corporation (Construction) (1984), 50 A.R. 311 (C.A.). Section 67(3) of the Act recognizes that there may be problems in this Court if an action is transferred to it and the documents filed in Provincial Court be the pleadings in this Court. However, where the Provincial Court documents are not sufficient in the case I do not believe the Court is restricted to ordering that the action be recommenced in this Court. Section 73 allows the application of the Rules of Court. Rule 222 allows the Court to order that the parties prepare issues where the pleadings do not sufficiently define the issues of fact. Rule 222 is appropriate to order that the issues be defined by the parties delivering statements, where an action is transferred to this Court and the documents from Provincial Court are not appropriate in the circumstances. 16. Purpose of Rule Manitoba has a similar rule. In Graham v. Canadian Premier Life Insurance Co. (1966), 57 W.W.R. 318 (Man. C.A.), Mr. Justice Freedman said at pp. 319-20: It is the function of the court to act judicially and not in an advisory or consultative capacity. The occasions on which a special case may be stated for the opinion of the court under Q.B.R. 204 are limited to those where a question of law arises upon facts which are either agreed or not in issue. In the present case, however, the facts are distinctly in issue, and counsel for the defendant expressly reserved the right, in the event of an adverse decision on the special case, to contest those facts. As a result, the court was being invited to participate in what might well have turned out to be simply an academic exercise. … the court should not enter by anticipation into a consideration of what might be the effect in point of law of circumstances or facts which have not yet been ascertained, established, or agreed upon… 17. Agreements as to Law Are Not Binding I share the view of the learned trial judge that the court is not bound thereby when it becomes apparent that the character of the document under question is a conclusion of law. Questions of law must always remain within the domain of the court. An agreement as to facts and an agreement which has the effect of establishing a fact in law which is contrary to the law, though honestly misconceived, do not stand in the same category. The latter, in my view, if detected, cannot be allowed to prevail. As a general rule no court of whatever level should permit itself to be used and knowingly adjudicate upon any issue presented by opposing litigants based on an erroneous premise; to do so would only serve to erode the credibility and prestige of the judicial system. Avco Delta Corp. v. Mackay, [1977] 5 W.W.R. 4 at 8 (Alta. C.A.).

sentences.text: Commentary § 7.1:1 Rule 7.1 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
Generally In Edmonton Flying Club v.
Edmonton Regional Airports Authority, 2013 ABCA 91, 2013 CarswellAlta 294, 544 A.R.
6, 77 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 389, the Court of Appeal discussed severing issues and Rule 7.1.

At paragraphs 30-31, the Justices Slatter and Rowbotham said: 30 The rules of civil procedure contemplate that every action will result in only one trial, where all issues will be decided: Judicature Act, RSA 2000, c.
Rule 7.1 does permit the severance of issues, but it is exceptional.
Prospects of speed, efficiency and economy from severed trials have often proved to be elusive: Gallant v Farries at paras.

An applicant who proposes to sever issues must demonstrate that it is clearly desirable to do so, and the legal test for severance is set accordingly: there must be a “real likelihood” or “good probability” of savings: Gallant v Farries at paras.
31 Therefore, a split trial must be one likely to achieve those aims which R.
7.1 lists: Gallant v Farries at para.
In other words, severing the trial must be likely to result in disposing of all or part of a claim, or substantially shortening the trial, or saving expense, or some combination thereof.
As the chambers judge recognized at para.
29, if it appears that there will be a significant overlap in the evidence to be called at the two phases of the trial, that is presumptively fatal to the application: Gallant v Farries at para.
And at paragraph 36: “… Severance should not be ordered in a way that prevents the defendant from putting forward all its defences: Potash Corp. of Saskatchewan Mining Ltd. v.
Allendale Mutual Insurance Co.
R.
184 at paras.
Does the “Exceptional Case Test” Still Apply?
In Envision Edmonton Opportunities Society v.
Edmonton (City), 2011 ABQB 29, 2011 CarswellAlta 72, 507 A.R.
L.R.
(5th) 1, Justice Moen concluded that the exceptional case test is no longer applicable in Alberta.
At paragraphs 49, 52–54, Moen, J. said: 49 Prior to the enactment of the New Rules, the applicable test in Alberta under Rule 221 was the “exceptional case” test: Esso Resources.

Has that test now been superseded by Rule 7.1(1)(a) and the Foundational Rules under the New Rules? … 52 As I set out above, the effect of the New Rules, Rule 7.1(1)(a) and Rule 1.2, are intended to force a shift to greater willingness on the part of the courts to grant remedies that will lead to more timely and cost-effective results.
53 I find that the “exceptional case” test, as applied in Alberta, is not consistent with the New Rules.
Approaching the analysis from the perspective that severance is available only in exceptional cases leads to the court focusing on finding reasons for not severing.
54 The wording of the New Rules, however, suggests that the focus should in fact be on finding reasons to sever.
Rule 7.1(1)(a) sets out grounds to grant severance, rather than factors or grounds to deny severance.
The suggestion is that where those grounds, or any one of them, are sufficiently strong, the court should grant severance.
This reading is consistent with the purposes set out in the Foundational Rule, which stress timely and cost-effective justice.
It is important to read the comments found in Gallant (Litigation Guardian of) v.
Farries, 2012 ABCA 98, 2012 CarswellAlta 539, 522 A.R.
13, 60 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 134 about the effect, if any, of R.
1.2 on the law interpreting R.
7.1 (see the annotation under R.

At paragraphs 8-13, 15-18, and 25-27, the Court said: 8 Counsel for the defendant suggested in oral argument that the court could decide this appeal largely on the facts and on the tests in R 7.1 of the Rules of Court.
I discuss that important topic in Part F below.
But that is not the approach which either the chambers judge or the plaintiff's counsel adopted.
Both relied heavily on a legal suggestion in Envision Edmonton Opportunities Society v Edmonton (City), 2011 ABQB 29, 507 AR 275, 44 Alta LR (5th) 1.
The facts in Envision were unusual, and the split there may have been proper.
But the suggestion there was broad: to reverse all the case law on splitting trials (in paras.
The case theorized that R 1.2 of the new Rules had effected a sea change (at least on this topic), so the prior case law on splitting off issues for separate trials could no longer apply.
The defendant's factum replies to that theory.
9 Since the suggestion by the plaintiff and the chambers judge could have far-ranging implications, it is better that the Court of Appeal now offer Bench and Bar some guidance on that legal topic.

10 I quote the parts of R 1.2 which are in issue here: 1.2(1) The purpose of these rules is to provide a means by which claims can be fairly and justly resolved in or by a court process in a timely and cost effective way.
(2) In particular, these rules are intended to be used …

(b) to facilitate the quickest means of resolving a claim at the least expense, … The Envision decision suggests that these paragraphs change the whole approach of the Rules of Court, and that therefore prior binding Alberta case law on splitting trials is repealed.
11 With respect, that suggestion is unclear.
Envision's legal hypothesis would follow logically only if the aim of the previous Rules had been significantly different.
Indeed that hypothesis would work only if the aim of the previous Rules was not speed and economy, but was delay and expense.
I do not agree with any such notion.
(It is not explicit in the Envision decision, only logically necessary.) 12 What is more, one need not speculate or extrapolate.
The aim of the previous case law about splitting trials and trying issues separately, was stated there explicitly.
The argument made by counsel for trying an issue separately was virtually always the same.
It predicted that the split would likely save time and money, by never having to try certain issues.
Of course that is the same theory which the plaintiff and the chambers judge advanced here.
The courts' reply to that theory was always to see whether the split really would save time and money in that individual case.
That is the same approach the defendant advocates here.
13 I will cite only a small selection of the huge body of authorities for the traditional law.
That law warns that such splits are a dangerous but alluring siren, often ending by wasting everyone's time and money, not saving it.
See Windsor Refrigeration Co v Branch Nominees[1961] Ch 375, 396, [1961] 1 All ER 277, 283 (CA); Elcana Acceptance v.
Richmond, infra; Ratcliffe v Nakonechny, 2003 ABQB 667, 23 Alta LR (4th) 21, 44 CPC (5th) 325; Canadian Cancer Society v.
Bank of Montreal (1966) 57 WWR 182, 186 (Alta CA); CMHC v.
Canative Housing Corp.
(1988) 90 AR 303, 304; Esso Resources v.
Stearns Catalytic (1991) 114 AR 27, 29 30 (CA) (paras.
9 11); Keg River Métis Settlement v.
A number of these cases are binding authority. … 15 Not one of the pre 2010 cases in the slightest rejects that consistent aim of saving time and money.
Quite the contrary: they expressly adopt the identical aim.
They show the dangers of hopeful theorizing.
They state that bitter experience shows that splits rarely achieve economy in practice; usually the result of the split (one way or the other) is to increase the time and money consumed.
Savings of time and expense by severing issues have consistently proven to be elusive: LKD v JB, infra (para.
To adopt Dr.
Johnson, splitting advocates wish hope to triumph over experience.
16 Of course splits are not forbidden, and occasionally there is good reason to think that one will save time and money.
For example, sometimes a simple readily extricable preliminary issue will take little time or money, and stands a good chance of ending the suit.
An expired clear limitation period, or some discrete condition precedent to suing (such as someone's permission) have been tried separately in the past.
17 In other words, all along everyone agreed on the aims of speed and economy, and all sought them.
The only disagreement was on whether a particular split would advance or retard those agreed objectives.
18 Therefore, Alberta's new Rules merely recite what everyone took for granted under the prior Rules; that speed and economy are important objectives.

So that statement of the tradition is no excuse for discarding all or even big parts of Alberta precedent. … 25 More specifically, general R 1.2 cannot supersede clear criteria on splitting trials in R 7.1.
Its subrule (1) reads as follows: [section omitted] If read mechanically and literally, R 7.1 on splits would offer no criteria, only aims.
But read in the modern purposive fashion, it means that a trial split must be one likely to achieve those aims which R 7.1 lists, not to thwart them.
And those same aims are just what the pre 2010 case law on splits requires.
26 My rejection of an interpretation of R 7.1 based solely on its precise words follows a rule which the Supreme Court of Canada has adopted in upwards of 60 recent decisions.
(An inventory may be found in S.
Beaulac and P.
A.
Côté (2006) 40 Rev Jur Thémis 131.) A recent example of this rule is A G Canada v.

Besides the exact wording of the legislation, one must also interpret it by weighing the context of its words, their history, the evils sought to be redressed, the aims of the legislation, and the scheme adopted by it to address them.
Not wishing to kill trees or spill ink, I merely refer to the citations and quotations in Brick Protection Corp v.
Provincial Treasurer of Alberta, 2011 ABCA 214, 510 AR 336 (paras.
27 Paragraph 54 of the Envision decision speaks both of R 1.2 and R 7.1.
If it suggests that R 7.1's own wording, apart from R 1.2, contains a radically new direction or new standard of proof, I cannot agree.
I see nothing of that sort in R 7.1 itself.
In Smigelski v.
Smigelski, 2015 ABCA 320, Madam Justice Rowbotham said: 6 Pursuant to Rule 7.1(1)(a) the Court may order an issue to be tried before trial for the purpose of:
(i) disposing of all or part of a claim
(ii) substantially shortening a trial; or
(iii) saving expense.
A trial should not be split unless the savings are clear or at least probable: Gallant v Farries, 2012 ABCA 98, 522 AR 13.

The chambers judge found that the savings were probable here as there was a “real good chance” that the trial on the issue of the pre-nuptial agreement could save considerable time and funds for the parties in the event the husband was successful.
7 Splitting trials is the exception, not the rule.

There may be situations where it is clear or probable that time and money could be saved by determining the validity and scope of a pre-nuptial agreement prior to a trial on the issue of spousal support.
However, where the claims overlap, the savings are less likely.
This is particularly so where the source of the payor's income for the purposes of spousal support is also one of the assets potentially available for division as matrimonial property.
This Court in Lakhoo v Lakhoo, 2014 ABCA 98, leave to appeal to SCC refused, [2014] SCCA No 203, considered a similar situation.

The Court allowed an appeal from a chambers judge's order bifurcating a trial where spousal support was at issue and disclosure of the payor's financial information would be required regardless of the validity of the pre-nuptial agreement.
In Schlichter v.

Pearce, 2022 ABQB 434, 2022 CarswellAlta 1601, Justice Richardson said: [6] The prerequisites to engaging this Rule are disjunctive, such that only one of the three needs to exist for the severance application to be considered.
The question is whether there is a real likelihood that one of the prerequisites can be satisfied (Gallant v Farries, 2012 ABCA 98 at para 31).

[7] The Respondent argues that once at least one of the prerequisites is found, the analysis then moves on to consider r 1.2 of the Alberta Rules of Court, in order to assess, on all the evidence available, whether severance of a claim is warranted.
In arriving at this final determination, he argues that the Court must consider that the aim of the Rules is to get to the merits as quickly, efficiently, inexpensively, and fairly as possible.

This approach was preferred in Envision Edmonton Opportunities Societies v Edmonton (City of), 2011 ABQB 29 at para 74 and Nowicki v Price, 2011 ABQB 133 at para 18, both decisions that immediately postdate the implementation of the current Rules in 2010.
[8] I disagree with the Respondent that this second step in the analysis is a required step.
This approach was rejected by the Alberta Court of Appeal in the subsequent decision of Gallant v Farries and this approach has not been adopted in any other appellate cases.

[9] In Gallant v Farries, the Court of Appeal held that the provisions of r 1.2 changed nothing from the prior regime, where speed and economy were already important objectives in civil litigation: (para 18 and 24).
The test remains a review of the criteria in r 7.1 and an assessment of whether a split trial is likely to achieve the aims of the section, and not to thwart them: (at para 25).
Although I am entitled to consider r 1.2 in applying r 7.1, there is no required second step to the analysis: NEP Canada ULC v MEC Op LLC, 2016 ABCA 201.
[10] The Appellant argues that exceptional circumstances are required to engage r 7.1.

The Respondent argues that the 2010 legislative amendments to the Rules, specifically the addition of r 1.2, results in the relaxation of the previous test that required exceptional circumstances before permitting severance of a claim.
[11] It is correct that the 2010 revision to the Rules removed the “exceptional circumstances” language from severance applications.

However, it remains the case that splitting a trial into its component parts is the exception to the general rule that civil actions will proceed to a single trial: LKD v JB, 2012 ABCA 72 at para 6: Smigelski v Smigelski, 2015 ABCA 320 at para 7.

[12] It is also correct that severance is an exception to the principle in civil procedure which contemplates that every action will result in only one trial, where all issues will be decided: Judicature Act, RSA 2000, c.
Rule 7.1 is an exception to this principle: Edmonton Flying Club v Edmonton Regional Airports Authority, 2013 ABCA 91, at para 30.
Two Stage Procedure Remains In Manson Insulation Products Ltd. v.

Crossroads C & I Distributors, 2011 ABQB 51, 2011 CarswellAlta 108, the Plaintiff (referred to as “New Manson”) brought an application for certain declarations regarding a distribution agreement between the Plaintiff and the Defendant.

The application was based “on the rules for preliminary determination of issues and summary judgment based on admissions.” In the course of addressing the issues before him, Justice Poelman referred to old Rule 221, and said, “[t]his rule clearly provided for a two-stage procedure and was applied in that manner by the authorities”: paragraph 19.
In respect of new rule 7.1, his Lordship said (at paragraphs 20–22): 20 In my view, the new rule also contemplates a two-stage procedure.
That is clear, first, from the plain words.
Rule 7.1(1) authorizes the court to order a question or issue to be heard, to define the question or issue and to give procedural directions.

Rule 7.1(3) is premised upon there having been an order under rule 7.1(1) and a determination made, and speaks only to the remedies available when “the Court is satisfied that its determination … substantially disposes of a claim or makes the trial of the issue unnecessary.” Importantly, the conditions needed for the remedies in rule 7.1(3) are not necessarily required for the court to order determination of a question or issue under rule 7.1 generally.

Preliminary determination of an issue might substantially shorten a trial or save expense, within the meaning of rule 7.1(1)(a), and thus merit an order that it be “heard or tried before it, at or after a trial,” while not substantially disposing of a claim or making trial unnecessary within the meaning of rule 7.1(3).
Thus, rule 7.1(3) is part of the overall system that rule 7.1 provides for determination of particular questions and issues; it does not operate independently as its own procedure.
21 Second, there are reasons of economy for both the parties and the judicial system that support a two-stage procedure.

The court should not be required to determine separately every question or issue in an action that the parties put before them, without first considering whether it would dispose of all or part of a claim, substantially shorten a trial or save expense.

Similarly, a responding party should not be put to the expense of contesting on evidence and law the very question or issue proposed to be separately heard or tried, before having the opportunity to make submissions on whether there should be a separate determination.

These considerations are consistent with the purpose and intention of the new rules as set out in rule 1.2, which emphasize resolution of claims in a timely and cost-effective way and discourage applications that do not achieve that purpose.
Preserving a two-stage procedure enables the court to ensure that separate determination of issues will occur only in proper cases.
22 New Manson has not applied for an order under rule 7.1(1).
Rather it has applied directly under rule 7.1(3), which assumes that the court has found that there should be a preliminary determination of the matters on which a declaration is sought.
For this reason alone, New Manson's application must fail.
Justice Poelman then considered an application under R.

7.1(1), and said (at paragraph 23): 23 If New Manson's application were to be treated as though it were under rule 7.1(1), it would be necessary to consider whether the proposed determination of the requested declaration would dispose of all or part of a claim, substantially shorten a trial or save expense.
While there are changes from the former rule 221 to the new rule 7.1, some of the authorities considering the former rule remain instructive.
In particular, I note the Court of Appeal's warnings about “piecemeal” determination of preliminary issues in Esso Resources Canada Limited v.
Stearns Catalytic Ltd.
Severance vs.
Summary Judgment In L.
Alberta, 2011 ABQB 771, 2011 CarswellAlta 2262, Graesser, J. said, at paragraphs 53-54, and 56–60: 53 The fact that severance might have been sought does not answer the question, however.
Severance seeks the court's direction that an issue be hived off the remaining claims and determined before other claims proceed.

Severance suggests that the issue to be tried will still be subject to disclosure of information procedures (record production and questioning), expert witness report exchanges and likely an alternative dispute resolution process (or waiver) under R.

54 Summary judgment does not require that there have been any record production or questioning, and the ADR requirement is not applicable to summary judgment, as it seeks to avoid a trial. … 56 Severance contemplates an order for an issue to be heard or tried “disposing of all or part of a claim” (R.
This wording is substantially the same as R.
57 In my view, these rules must be read together, as offering the parties choices of a course of action.

If a party believes that resolution of one issue amongst many might “dispose of all or part of a claim, substantially shorten the trial, or save expense”, but the party still requires record production, questioning, expert report production and a trial, severance may be the appropriate route to follow.

58 If the party believes that an issue can be determined in a summary way (i.e. without trial), because there have been admissions of fact or the only evidence necessary is in the form of authentic records, summary judgment may be the appropriate route to follow.
59 The foundational rules emphasize the objectives of fairness, justice, efficiency, economy and proportionality.

Having regard to the high financial and emotional cost of litigation and the time usually taken by the full litigation process, parties should be encouraged to pursue strategies which may shorten the proceedings.
That is one of the reasons mandatory ADR has been introduced.

60 I note that the cases on severance which have been decided since the new rules came into effect in November, 2010, (Envision, Nowicki and Ponich) appear to be lessening the barriers to severance which existed under the old rules.
In particular, I refer to Veit J.'s comments in Ponich, at para.

9: • New Rule 7.1 is considerably broader in scope than the Rules it replaces and explicitly authorizes the granting of orders designed either to dispose of part of a claim or to save expense; • the new foundational rules in the Rules of Court require a court to consider how trials can be heard as expeditiously as possible … 5.
Must Facts Alleged Be Proved?
Generally, the application is brought by a party who is of the view that, even on the facts as alleged by the other side, a decisive point of law will be decided in favour of the applicant.
Therefore, one must take the facts as alleged by the respondent.
The first question is as to what materials my decision should be based on.

The answer to that question is that, in this case, the allegations of fact alleged in the pleadings of the plaintiff are to be taken as true and the allegations of fact in the pleadings of the defendant are not to be regarded.
It was so held in the Bank of Ottawa v.
Township of Roxborough et al.
511, a decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal, in which decision Moss, C.J.O., at pp.
518-9, said the following: For the purposes of the argument as to want of jurisdiction, the allegations of the statement of defence ought not to be regarded.
Unless this were so, a defendant might support his point of law by putting upon record statements which were untrue in fact and which he would utterly fail to support by evidence at a trial.
No doubt the parties might admit all the essential facts that could be proved on both sides and thus reduce the matter to a pure point of law, but that is not this case.

Looking, therefore, at the allegations of the statement of claim, which the plaintiffs undertake to prove, if permitted, and assuming, as for the purposes of the discussion of the point of law it should be, that they are true, I am unable to say at present that the High Court has not jurisdiction to entertain the action.
That case was followed in Green v.
Spencer et al., [1939] O.W.N.
47 … in which case Kelly, J., at p.
48, stated the law succinctly as follows: It has been laid down in Bank of Ottawa v.
Township of Roxborough (1909), 18 O.L.R.

511, that in considering the point of law allegations of fact in the pleadings of the party raising the point of law cannot be regarded, and that all allegations of fact alleged in the opposite pleading are to be taken as true.

The point of law must be one arising out of facts clearly admitted in the pleadings. … It would appear therefore that the issue should be decided on the assumption that the facts set out in the plaintiff's pleadings are true … It is clear, therefore, that the point of law raised must be clear and the decision not contingent on the resolution of any dispute as to facts … … that which is raised in a reply should be considered.
Therefore, if as a result of a reply a factual issue necessary for deciding the point of law remains unresolved, the point of law cannot be decided on a motion under Rule 124.
[Alberta, R.
Piuti v.
Toronto (Board of Education) (1974), 6 O.R.
It can be concluded that if the facts as pleaded by the respondent are not clear, then a R.
7.1 application is inappropriate.

A preliminary question of law under Rule 220 of the Supreme Court Rules must be decided by assuming for the purpose of the motion only, that all facts alleged in the material before the court are true …McCarthy v.
Calgary Roman Catholic Separate School District No.
Note that the court does not rely on the allegations of fact contained in the applicant's pleadings.
Plaintiff sued three defendants for falsely imprisoning him in the Ontario Hospital at London.

One of the defendants moved for leave to set down for hearing before trial the following point of law raised in the defence, “…. that plaintiff's action is barred on the ground that he has brought this action without first obtaining the consent of the Attorney-General of Ontario as required by the Mental Hospitals Act, R.S.O.

10.” Kelly J. said that no point of law arose on the pleadings within the meaning of Rule 122, for nowhere in plaintiff's pleadings did it appear that consent of the Attorney-General was not obtained, and defendant could not have a point of law determined under the Rule upon allegations of fact in his own pleadings.
Green v.
Spencer, [1939] 1 D.L.R.
S.C.), per Kelly J.
Disputed Facts The courts have often held that a preliminary question of law, or similar split of the case, must not be used where the result can depend upon the facts.
Armstrong v.
McLaughlin Estate (1995), 178 A.R.
125 (C.A.), at 126, per Côté J.A.
Effect of R.
7.1 Order With all due respect to the learned chambers judge, he misconceived the effect of a decision on a point of law under R.

He erred in concluding that it was open to the plaintiff to adduce further evidence at trial on the question decided by Dechene J., upon which the trial judge could make a different disposition of the point of law.
That question decided by Dechene J., and the Court of Appeal was res judicata, even though these decisions may not have been final determination of all the issues in the action.
The hearing of a point of law under R.
220 is surely not a mere procedure for testing the waters for prospective litigation with a view to guiding the parties into secure legal positions, for that would clearly be an abuse of process.
The courts do not decide hypothetical questions.
Such a hearing is an alternative route for disposition of a point of law for the purpose of the trial.
The words in R.
220 “otherwise it shall be disposed of at trial” contemplate that such a disposition shall be made at the hearing.
The facts admitted on the submission of a point of law for determination under R.
220 are deemed to be all of the facts relevant to the point of law as if they had been established in evidence on that issue at the trial had the issue proceeded to trial.
The parties are bound by those facts on that point to the same extent that they would have been had the facts been found by the trial judge on evidence adduced before him.
A judicial determination of a point of law on the admitted facts has the same binding effect that it would have had if made at the conclusion of the trial.
Once entered the decision operates as an estoppel by res judicata if the same point is sought to be relitigated or reargued by the same parties, whether in the same action or another.

The learned chambers judge was of the opinion that the decision of Dechene J. and that of the Court of Appeal affirming it did not create estoppel by res judicata because it was not the final judgment in the action.
But it is not only the final judgment in an action which will be res judicata.
Estoppel by res judicata is created by any judicial decision which “finally” determines the rights of the parties inter se.
Guarantee Trust Co. v.
Bailey (1987), 52 Alta.
L.R.
Are Questions on Admissibility of Evidence Appropriate?
While this was neither raised nor argued by the parties in the appeal, I should like to add that, in my opinion, the question placed before Mr.
Justice Girgulis being one of admissibility of evidence should normally have been dealt with by the trial judge.
I doubt that it was the proper subject for determination on a point of law under R.
220 unless by the trial judge himself.
This judgment should not be read as endorsing the procedure followed here, the point being left open for future determination.
Guarantee Trust Co. v.
Bailey, supra, at 303.

Granting Security under Rule I see nothing in the rules under consideration that would make it improper for a chambers Judge to exact some form of security as a condition of granting the order requested here.
Perhaps as a general rule there would be no need for such a requirement.

It would appear that the learned chambers judge had some anxiety that should the issue of liability become involved in a series of appeals resulting in ultimate delay, the appellant's claim for damages on the counterclaim if finally held to be a valid one, should be protected at least to some extent.
I can see nothing wrong in such an approach.
I can see nothing wrong either in the requiring of a bond of indemnity as a condition to the granting of the relief sought under the special circumstances of the present case.
Karlsen Shipping Co. v.
Sefel J. & Associates Ltd.
341 (C.A.), at 347-48, per Morrow J.
Leave Required One must first seek leave to have a matter heard.
Generally, all substantive issues in a defended action should be decided at trial.
There are various exceptions to that.
One of them is found in Rule 221.
In my view, Rule 221 involves a two step procedure identical to Rule 220.
In Town of Spruce Grove v.
Yellowhead Regional Library Board (1983), 44 A.R.
408, Laycraft, J.A., states at p.
50: Rule 220 of the Rules of Court enables the parties to pose a preliminary point of law for determination by the court only ‘with leave of the court’.
Application is made in chambers for leave and, if it is granted, the questions are formulated.
That procedure does not appear to have been followed in this case.
Rather the parties simply appeared in Queen's Bench chambers by agreement and proceeded to argue the three questions they had devised.
The chambers judge apparently assumed an order had been made giving leave and proceeded directly to the questions.
Had the prescribed procedure been followed, leave might well have been refused.
Not only do the points of law raised go beyond the pleadings, but there appears to be no compelling reason not to bring all parts of the case forward at the same time.
The evidence in this case will surely not take more than few minutes to adduce.
All issues could then have been resolved at once rather than in the present fragmented fashion.

Although the terminology of the two rules is somewhat different I believe that both involve a preliminary screening process by the Court to determine whether it is appropriate that some issue be tried other than at trial.
I do not agree that Rule 221 allows a party to make an application for a determination of an issue without more.
Rule 221 says the Court may order any issue “to be tried before, at or after the trial”.
Without such an order a party cannot just jump in and try to have the merits of an issue adjudicated on before trial.
Skagos v.
Emery Jamieson (1986), 72 A.R.
231 ((Master)), at 239, per Master Funduk.
Same Judge Need Not Hear Severed Trials In Jen-Col Construction Ltd. v.
Parkland (County) No.
352 (Q.B.), the liability issue had been severed from the quantum of damage issue.
Veit, J. was asked whether the same judge had to hear both trials.
At p.
354, her Ladyship said: The liability trial judge is not seized of the damages issue.
The court has discretion to decide whether it is seized of the completion of the trial.
In making such a decision, the court should have regard to at least the following factors: efficiency, utilization of court resources, and potential prejudice.
In this case, there was no important evidence led on the liability trial that dealt in any way with the issue of damages.
Nor were there any real findings on credibility that would bind any other judge hearing the liability trial.
There would be no prejudice either way to either of the parties.
Therefore, on the facts of this case, the Chief Justice will make the assignment of the judge who will hear the remaining issues.
Questions of Mixed Law and Fact However, I respectfully agree with the decision of Cooke J., on a similar application by a hospital in Jaffer v.
Schultze (February 5, 1991), Edmonton 8803 14161 (Alta.
Q.B.), in which he concluded that the use of the related R.
221 for the determination of preliminary points is not appropriate where the issue is one of mixed fact and law, in denying the application.
Brown (Next Friend of) v.
University of Alberta Hospital (1995), 31 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 260 (Q.B.), at 264, per Bielby J.
Applications Concerning Limitation Dates If there are no disputes of fact limitation defences are probably susceptible to a pre-trial adjudication.
If a limitation defence is successful that concludes the action.
A successful limitation defence obviates the necessity to deal with the merits of the claim in any fashion.
Skagos v.
Emery Jamieson (1986), 72 A.R.
231 (Master), at 239, per Master Funduk.

Limitations of Rule We agree that rule 221 does not authorize a trial judge to send out, as it were, a part of the trial in a case where the issues sent out are inextricably bound up with the issues raised in the pleadings that he must finally determine, and that involve questions of fact and, probably, questions of credibility.
Jackson v.
Trimac Industries Ltd.
Issue not defined by pleadings In Snowbird Rentals Ltd. v.
B.T.U.
Panels Ltd.
120 (Master), the court invoked R.
222 to order the preparation of pleadings for an action transferred to the Court of Queen's Bench from Provincial Court.
In quoting Canadian Overnite Courier (1983) Ltd. v.
Jasper Printing Group Ltd.
(January 15, 1985), Doc.
8403 25681 (Q.B.), Master Funduk said at p.
122: In this Court pleadings define the issues and determine the scope of examinations for discovery.
In addition, any judgment given must be based on the issues placed before the Court by the pleadings: Creditel of Canada v.
Terrace Corporation (Construction) (1984), 50 A.R.
Section 67(3) of the Act recognizes that there may be problems in this Court if an action is transferred to it and the documents filed in Provincial Court be the pleadings in this Court.
However, where the Provincial Court documents are not sufficient in the case I do not believe the Court is restricted to ordering that the action be recommenced in this Court.
Section 73 allows the application of the Rules of Court.
Rule 222 allows the Court to order that the parties prepare issues where the pleadings do not sufficiently define the issues of fact.

Rule 222 is appropriate to order that the issues be defined by the parties delivering statements, where an action is transferred to this Court and the documents from Provincial Court are not appropriate in the circumstances.
Purpose of Rule Manitoba has a similar rule.
In Graham v.
Canadian Premier Life Insurance Co.
C.A.), Mr.
Justice Freedman said at pp.
319-20: It is the function of the court to act judicially and not in an advisory or consultative capacity.
The occasions on which a special case may be stated for the opinion of the court under Q.B.R.
204 are limited to those where a question of law arises upon facts which are either agreed or not in issue.

In the present case, however, the facts are distinctly in issue, and counsel for the defendant expressly reserved the right, in the event of an adverse decision on the special case, to contest those facts.

As a result, the court was being invited to participate in what might well have turned out to be simply an academic exercise. … the court should not enter by anticipation into a consideration of what might be the effect in point of law of circumstances or facts which have not yet been ascertained, established, or agreed upon… 17.

Agreements as to Law Are Not Binding I share the view of the learned trial judge that the court is not bound thereby when it becomes apparent that the character of the document under question is a conclusion of law.
Questions of law must always remain within the domain of the court.
An agreement as to facts and an agreement which has the effect of establishing a fact in law which is contrary to the law, though honestly misconceived, do not stand in the same category.
The latter, in my view, if detected, cannot be allowed to prevail.

As a general rule no court of whatever level should permit itself to be used and knowingly adjudicate upon any issue presented by opposing litigants based on an erroneous premise; to do so would only serve to erode the credibility and prestige of the judicial system.
Avco Delta Corp. v.
Mackay, [1977] 5 W.W.R.
4 at 8 (Alta.
