paragraphs.text: Commentary § 7.2:1 Rule 7.2 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 7.2. 1. Overview In Sticks and Stones Communications Inc. v. Hole's Greenhouses & Gardens Ltd., 2015 ABQB 774, Justice Graesser gave the following overview of summary judgment applications: 30 The guiding law on summary judgment has changed over the last short while, with the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7. That decision, especially at para 28, directed a fresh approach to summary judgment and summary dismissal, has effectively done away with the old tests for summary judgment: “beyond doubt” or “plain and obvious”. 31 The Alberta Court of Appeal applied Hryniak in Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway, 2014 ABCA 108. 32 The Masters have, in Alberta, been the primary interpreters and appliers of Hyrniak because of the nature of their work. Master Schlosser synthesized the approach to summary judgment applications where there are contested facts in 1214777 Alberta Ltd v 480955 Alberta Ltd At paras 16 and 17 he stated: [16] If we put these decisions together, the approach that now ought to be taken toward summary determination is as follows. I am drawing remarks of Master MacLeod in the Pammett, [2014] O.J. No. 1968 decision and those of Wakeling, J., (as he then was) in the Proper Cat [2013] A.J. No. 707 case. The new approach has been described as the “roadmap approach”. As I see it, the Alberta roadmap is as follows: [17] The starting point (as found in the Windsor decision para. 13 and Hryniak at para. 49) is “to examine the record to see if a disposition that is fair and just to both parties can be made on the exis ting record”. The court is to look at the record and the dispute to decide whether it is essential to the resolution of the dispute that the court see the witnesses. If the answer is yes, the matter must go to trial. If the initial answer is “no”, the court is to engage in a six step process: 1. The court is to presume that the best evidence from both sides is before the court. (e.g. Canada v. Lameman, 2008 SCC 14 (CanLII), [2008] 1 SCR 372, at 378 and 382). The decided cases tell us that summary judgment applications have to be decided on the evidence before the court and not on what the evidence might be. Parties are required to put their best foot forward. This reinforces the importance of treating summary judgment applications advisedly and with due caution. The only caveat that might apply here is that if the summary judgment application is before a Master and the losing party does not like the Master's opinion, it is not so difficult to patch up the evidence on appeal. 2. As a corollary to number 1, the court is to ask whether a negative inference can be drawn from the absence of evidence on certain points. 3. Next, the court should look at the complete package and ask whether all of the evidence is admissible. Rule 13.18 (3), for example, tells us that we can't use hearsay for a final application. 4. Next, the court should ask whether there is a conflict in the evidence and, if so, whether, (a) the conflict has been resolved on cross examination: Janvier v 834474 Alberta Ltd., 2010 ABQB 800 (CanLII), or, (b), whether the evidence giving rise to the conflict is purely self-serving and is otherwise unsupported: Guaranty v. Gordon, [1999] S.C.J. No. 60. Self serving evidence does not give rise to a triable issue. 5. The next step is to examine the evidence. As Master MacLeod said in the Pammett decision: [28] There are subtle distinctions here. The court may assess the sufficiency of the evidence admissibility of evidence and reliability of evidence without access to enhanced fact finding powers. The court may also apply the law to the facts without deciding a genuine question of law. • (emphasis added) 33 Assessing the sufficiency of the evidence will also involve considering whether the issue can fairly be decided on the factual record before the court (Tottrup v Clearwater Municipal District (99) (2007) 2006 ABCA 380 (CanLII), 68 Alta L.R. (4th) 237 at 242 and Gayton v Lacasse, 2010 ABCA 123 (CanLII) at para. 11). 6. Having performed that evidentiary exercise, as Master MacLeod further says in the Pammett case: (and see Proper Cat at paras. 61–64, 69): [31] A plaintiff will be entitled to judgment if the plaintiff can prove all elements of the cause of action and the defendant either has no defence or is missing critical elements of proof necessary to maintain that defence. A defendant will be entitled to judgment if the plaintiff cannot prove an essential element of its cause or if the defendant has a complete defence. 34 Proper Cat was approved by the Court of Appeal in Access Mortgage Corporation (2004) Limited v Arres Capital Inc., 2014 ABCA 280. 35 In WP v Alberta, 2014 ABCA 404, the Court of Appeal stated at para 26: [26] Summary judgment is therefore no longer to be denied solely on the basis that the evidence discloses a triable issue. The question is whether there is in fact any issue of “merit” that genuinely requires a trial, or conversely whether the claim or defence is so compelling that the likelihood it will succeed is very high such that it should be determined summarily: Windsor at para 16; Beier at paras 56, 59-68 and 70. 36 The Court of Appeal further discussed Hyrniak in 776826 Alberta Ltd. v Ostrowercha, 2015 ABCA 49, holding at para 11 to 13: [11] Stated another way, in order for the non-moving party's case to have merit, there must be a genuine issue of a potentially decisive material fact in the case which cannot be summarily found against the non-moving party on the record revealed by the “fair and just process”. The mere assertion of a position by the non-moving party in a pleading or otherwise, or the mere hope of the non-moving party that something will turn up at a trial, does not suffice. The key is whether the circumstances require a viva voce evidence in order to properly resolve the case: see Canada v Lameman, 2008 SCC 14 (CanLII) at paras 10 to 11, [2008] 1 SCR 372. [12] The concept of “merit” in this respect is to be distinguished from the test for striking out pleadings under Rule 3.68 which involves deciding “whether there is any reasonable prospect that the claim will succeed, erring on the side of generosity in permitting novel claims to proceed.”: compare Ernst v Alberta (Energy Resources Conservation Board), 2014 ABCA 285 (CanLII) at paras 13 to 15, 85 CELR (3d) 39, under motion [2014] SCCA No 497 (QL). [13] As to the substantive aspect of the test, then, this Court has also put the test for summary dismissal into the following terms in W.P., at para. 26: Summary judgment is therefore no longer to be denied solely on the basis that the evidence discloses a triable issue. The question is whether there is in fact any issue of “merit” that genuinely requires a trial, or conversely whether the claim or defence is so compelling that the likelihood it will succeed is very high such that it should be determined summarily: Windsor at para 16; Beier at paras 56, 59–68 and 70. 37 In Attila Dogan Construction v AMEC Americas Limited, 2015 ABQB 120, Wittmann CJ added to the interpretation of Hyrniak at para 52: [52] To this set of principles I would add some further points of direct application to the Summary Applications sought here. It is important to understand that the principle of proportionality and what has been described as the less stringent test for summary judgment in Alberta does not affect the evidentiary requirements for such applications. As discussed in further detail below, affidavit evidence sworn in support of summary judgment must comply with the provisions of the ARC and these are unaffected by Hryniak and Windsor. Furthermore, a self-serving affidavit in and of itself is not sufficient to create a triable issue in the absence of detailed facts and supporting evidence: Guarantee Co. of North America v Gordon Capital Corp., 1999 CanLII 664 (SCC), [1999] 3 SCR 423, at para 31. Finally, the principle of proportionality will require that the procedure used to adjudicate the dispute should fit the nature of the claim, but proportionality has more than one aspect. The magnitude of the claim in terms of monetary value may have some place in this analysis, but the nature of the claim will as well. It has been recognized, for example, that disputes over the interpretation of an instrument, such as a contract, may lend themselves particularly well to summary judgment: Tottrup v Clearwater (Municipal District 99), 2006 ABCA 380 (CanLII). In Elkow v. Sana, 2015 ABQB 803, at paragraph 60, Justice Graesser affirmed his comments in Sticks and Stones Communications Inc. v. Hole's Greenhouses & Gardens Ltd., 2015 ABQB 774, and then said: 63 If the court determines that viva voce evidence is not required, then the court must engage in a six-step analysis to determine whether a matter is suitable for summary judgment: Windsor at para 13, Hryniak at para 49, 1214777 Alberta Ltd. v 480955 Alberta Ltd, 2014 ABQB 301, Beier v Proper Cat Construction Ltd, 2013 ABQB 351 [Proper Cat]: 1. The court is to presume that the best evidence from both sides is before the court. (e.g. Canada v Lameman, [2008] 1 SCR 372, at 378 and 382). The decided cases tell us that summary judgment applications have to be decided on the evidence before the court and not on what the evidence might be. Parties are required to put their best foot forward. This reinforces the importance of treating summary judgment applications advisedly and with due caution. The only caveat that might apply here is that if the summary judgment application is before a Master and the losing party does not like the Master's opinion, it is not so difficult to patch up the evidence on appeal. 2. As a corollary to number 1, the court is to ask whether a negative inference can be drawn from the absence of evidence on certain points. 3. Next, the court should look at the complete package and ask whether all of the evidence is admissible. Rule 13.18 (3), for example, tells us that we can't use hearsay for a final application. 4. Next, the court should ask whether there is a conflict in the evidence and, if so, whether, (a) the conflict has been resolved on cross examination: Janvier v 834474 Alberta Ltd., 2010 ABQB 800, or, (b), whether the evidence giving rise to the conflict is purely self-serving and is otherwise unsupported: Guaranty v. Gordon, [1999] 3 SCR 423. Self-serving evidence does not give rise to a triable issue. 5. The next step is to examine the evidence. As Master MacLeod said in the Pammett[2014] O.J. No. 1968 decision: [28] There are subtle distinctions here. The court may assess the sufficiency of the evidence admissibility of evidence and reliability of evidence without access to enhanced fact finding powers. The court may also apply the law to the facts without deciding a genuine question of law. Assessing the sufficiency of the evidence will also involve considering whether the issue can fairly be decided on the factual record before the court (Tottrup v. Clearwater Municipal District (99) (2007) 68 Alta L.R. (4th) 237 at 242 and Gayton v. Lacasse, 2010 ABCA 123 at para. 11). 6. Having performed that evidentiary exercise, as Master MacLeod further says in the Pammett case: (and see Proper Cat at paras. 61–64, 69): [31] A plaintiff will be entitled to judgment if the plaintiff can prove all elements of the cause of action and the defendant either has no defence or is missing critical elements of proof necessary to maintain that defence. A defendant will be entitled to judgment if the plaintiff cannot prove an essential element of its cause or if the defendant has a complete defence. (1214777 Alberta Ltd at para 17.) 64 The law on summary judgment now encourages summary judgment wherever it is reasonably possible. That is the obvious result of the enormous costs of litigation and the private and public resources necessarily employed to hold a trial. In Mackey v. Squair, 2015 ABQB 329, Justice Topolniski also approved Master Schlosser's summary in 1214777 Alberta Ltd. v. 480955 Alberta Ltd., 2014 ABQB 301 (Master). Justice Dario, in D. (D.) v. Calgary Counselling Centre, 2017 ABQB 95, 2017 CarswellAlta 219, also approved Master Schlosser's summary. 2. Burden of Proof In Rudichuk v. Genesis Land Development Corp., 2017 ABQB 285, 2017 CarswellAlta 707 (Master), Master Robertson discussed the burden of proof on a summary judgment application: 25 As is often the case in summary judgment applications, there is some debate over whether the plaintiffs have satisfied their burden sufficient to require the defendant to respond, and then whether the defendant's response was sufficient to establish that there is “an issue of merit that genuinely requires a trial”. In a summary judgment application, there is a burden to be met by the applicant and if it is met, the burden shifts to the respondent: Murphy Oil Company Ltd v Predator Corporation Ltd, 2006 ABCA 69, 384 A.R. 251 at para. 25; Canada (Attorney General) v. Lameman, [2008] 1 S.C.R. 372, 2008 SCC 14 at para. 11. Although it may be said that the non-moving party has no legal persuasive burden to discharge, the non-moving party may be at risk of losing if it fails to present a version of the facts inconsistent with that relied upon by the applicant: Murphy Oil, Lameman and Beier v Proper Cat Construction Ltd, 2013 ABQB 351 at para. 67. 26 At para.63 of Beier, Wakeling, J.A. gave an example particularly relevant here: he used the circumstance of a wrongful dismissal claim where the employment agreement provided for an obligation to pay a certain amount of money upon termination. Upon proving the agreement and the failure of the employer to comply, the plaintiff would be entitled to summary judgment. 27 In a wrongful dismissal claim where “just cause” is pled as the defence, as here, the primary burden is on the employer to prove that there was just cause. This is, at its core, simply an example of the proposition that he who asserts must prove, which applies across all areas of law unless there is a specific reverse onus. See, for example Garry v. Canada, 2007 ABCA 234 at para. 8; Workum v. Canada Customs and Revenue Agency, 2005 FC 991 (CanLII), 2005 F.C. 991; Totem Electric Ltd. v. Humford Developments Ltd., 1986 CanLII 1611 (AB QB), 68 A.R. 217, [1986] A.J. No. 146 (M.C.); and Slater v. Burgoin, 2001 ABCA 213 (CanLII) at paragraph 12. 28 Accordingly, an employer who asserts that there was just cause for dismissal must prove it. At trial, a plaintiff theoretically need only prove that he or she was employed, the terms of compensation, the factors that should be considered in assessing damages, that he or she was dismissed allegedly for cause, and then the employer is called upon to prove the case that there was just cause. 29 This has long been the law, and in my view it has a bearing on the analysis of the adequacy or inadequacy of the evidence provided in support of, and in response to, an application for summary judgment. 3. Questioning and document production and summary judgment applications In Diane Jonsson v. 1920341 Alberta Ltd., 2024 ABKB 184, Justice Bercov said: [12] Whether questioning and document production should proceed prior to the hearing of a summary judgment application is a discretionary decision under the rules. That discretion must be exercised giving due consideration to the purposes of Part 5, which includes discouraging conduct that improperly delays proceedings and increases costs: P. Burns Resources Limited v Honourable Patrick Burns Memorial Trust, 2015 ABCA 390, para 9. [13] A summary judgement motion must be judged based on the pleadings and the materials before the Court. A motion for summary judgment cannot be defeated by vague references or suppositions about what might be proved in the future: Canada (Attorney General) v Lameman, 2008 SCC 14, at para 19. [14] While a plaintiff cannot oppose summary judgment by arguing that evidence supporting the claim may arise during questioning, where the nature of the action is such that the evidence supporting the claim is in the sole possession of the defendant, the plaintiff is more likely to require questioning and disclosure of documents to be able to respond to a summary judgment application: P. Burns Resources Limited v Honourable Patrick Burns Memorial Trust, 2015 ABCA 390, para 8. 4. When to File Evidence in Response to Summary Judgment Application In Soler & Palau Canada Inc. v. Meyer's Sheet Metal Ltd., 2012 ABQB 496, 2012 CarswellAlta 1327, 545 A.R. 391, 77 Alta. L.R. (5th) 194 (Master), Master Hanebury said, at paragraphs 53-54: 53 The question of if and when evidence should be filed in response to a summary judgment application has been considered by the Courts on a number of occasions. Master Funduk, in an often cited case, Tucson Properties Ltd. v. Sentry Resources Ltd. [1982] A.J. No. 775, said it best: Whether a defendant can satisfy the burden imposed on him by the Rule merely by relying on his pleading, being the statement of defence, depends upon the issues raised in the pleading. If a defendant raises an issue of law in his statement of defence, that may be sufficient to meet the burden, if the court is of the view the issue of law raised is not beyond all doubt. If a defendant raises issues of fact in his statement of defence, that alone is not sufficient to meet the burden imposed on him. If a statement of defence raises issues of fact it is because of the allegations of fact in the statement of defence. Allegations of fact are just that, allegations. They are not evidence. A pleading is not evidence. If a defendant could rely on the allegations of fact in his statement of defence to meet the burden imposed by the Rule, it would make the Rule sterile. All that would be required is that the draftsman be astute enough to draft a statement of defence which raises issues of fact by making appropriate allegations of fact. If there is no evidence to support the issues the defendant raises in his defence, there is nothing for the court to weigh. The scales tip entirely in one direction, that direction being in favour of the plaintiff. If there is some evidence to support the issues the defendant raises, the court must then weigh that evidence and decide whether the plaintiff's claim is beyond all doubt. 54 This decision is under the former rules of Court. However it has been cited approvingly in relation to the new Rules of Court, and by the Supreme Court of Canada: Hall v. HSBC Capital (Canada) Inc., 2012 ABQB 114, para. 34; Canada (Attorney General) v. Lameman, 2008 SCC 14, para. 11; and see as well Lorne H. Reed & Associates Ltd. v. ProMax Energy Inc., 2003 ABQB 121, para. 12. See also: Jager Industries Inc. v. Canadian Occidental Petroleum Ltd., 2000 ABQB 592, para. 23. 5. When to cross-examine on applicant's affidavit In Clearbakk Energy Services Inc v. Sunshine Oilsands Ltd, 2022 ABQB 347, 2022 CarswellAlta 1243, additional reasons 2022 ABQB 506, reversed 2022 ABCA 386, additional reasons 2023 ABCA 96, Justice Jones disagreed with Master Prowse's criticism of the practice of cross-examining an applicant's deponent prior to filing a responsive affidavit (for Master Prowse's comments, see: Clearbakk Energy Services Inc. v. Sunshine Oilsands Ltd., 2021 ABQB 866, 2021 CarswellAlta 2721, reversed 2022 ABQB 347, additional reasons 2022 ABQB 506, reversed 2022 ABCA 386, additional reasons 2023 ABCA 96 (Master) at paragraphs 6–8). Justice Jones said: [6] First, the Master was of the opinion that Sunshine should have filed its own affidavit in response to Clearbakk's application. While the Master acknowledged that the Alberta Rules of Court, unlike those in other jurisdictions, do not require a responding affidavit, he felt that cross-examining Clearbakk's affiant before filing a responding affidavit was a waste of time. He also believed that, by proceeding in this manner, Sunshine was in breach of its obligations under Rule 1.2(3)(a). The Master's view was that this procedure ensured that the litigation would become unnecessarily lengthy and expensive. [7] I do not agree. While there may well be circumstances in which filing a responding affidavit is necessary or more efficient, that will not always be so. It is significant that our Rules do not require this. So long as it is compliant with the Rules, litigation strategy is to be determined by counsel and Sunshine was entitled to proceed as it did. Though Justice Jones' decision was overturned (see: Clearbakk Energy Services Inc v. Sunshine Oilsands Ltd, 2022 ABCA 386, additional reasons 2023 ABCA 96), the Court of Appeal did say, at paragraph 14: “Sunshine decided not to file evidence in response [to Clearbakk's affidavit] and instead relied on its cross-examination of Clearbakk's affidavit, as it was entitled to do.” 6. The Interplay between Summary Judgment and R. 7.1 In McKenzie v. Smith, 2016 ABQB 114 (Master), the Plaintiffs purchased a residential property from the Defendants. The Defendants did not tell the Plaintiffs that there was a history of sewer pipe blockages caused by tree roots encroaching on the sewer lines beyond the property boundary, and that the City of Edmonton had put the property on a City Maintenance Program under the terms of which the City would periodically seek permission to enter the property to take preventative action. Several months after the Plaintiffs took possession, the house suffered a sewer backup as a result of tree root encroachment. The Plaintiffs sued alleging a latent defect. The Plaintiffs brought an application for summary judgment on the issue of liability only. In relation to damages, they sought an order directing an assessment of damages. Master Schulz found a latent defect in the property, but had to consider how the Court should approach a summary judgment application which is only directed at liability (thereby involving R. 7.1) The learned Master said: 42 The issue to be addressed here is the effect of the Hyrniak approach on a summary judgment application to deal with liability only. Unfortunately, neither counsel addressed this question in their written briefs and counsel for the Vendors raised it at oral argument by handing up a copy of the decision of Swan Group Inc v Bishop, 2013 ABCA 29 (“Swan”). Handing up cases that are not addressed in written argument does a disservice to the Court and to opposing counsel. There was little oral argument on this issue but it is a live issue that must be addressed. 43 Counsel for the Vendors argues that our Court of Appeal has counselled against separating issues in matters more conveniently tried in one piece: Swan at para 35 referring to Gallant v Farries, 2012 ABCA 98 (“Gallant”). 44 Gallant is a detailed and thoughtful discussion of the application of the law on splitting trials. Among other things, Gallant concludes that the cases decided before the introduction of the 2010 Rules of Court are still applicable (See section C of Gallant) and confirms that the warnings contained in those prior cases are still applicable. It reviews the purpose and intention of the Rules as set out in Rule 1.2 and focuses in particular on the reference in Rule 1.2 to the facilitation of the quickest means of resolving a claim at the least expense. 45 The Gallant decision goes on at length to discuss the dangers of splitting a trial into two (or more) segments (See paragraphs 13, 23, and 54 and the cases cited therein). In particular, it raises the spectre of numerous appeals of the different segments defeating any well-intentioned goal of saving time and costs. It cautions the Court to recognize the reality of appeals (See paragraphs 29 and 32 to 47). 46 This caution and concern must be weighed against the subsequent decision in Hyrniak and the subsequent cases from our Court of Appeal that follow Hyrniak. Should the possibility of an appeal hold the Court hostage and prevent it from deciding an issue on summary judgment that, in the words of Hyrniak, “is fair and just to both parties … on the existing record by using that alternative method for adjudication”? Should the fear of every possible appeal scenario prevent the Court from ever deciding to proceed with anything other than a full trial of all issues? 47 In my opinion, there is a difference between splitting a trial into two, for example a trial on liability followed by a trial on quantum, and using summary judgment to determine liability and directing an assessment of damages. This is especially so where there is no overlap between the issues of liability and damages. In this case, there is no overlap. Everyone agrees that the sewer back up occurred. Everyone agrees that the “before” condition of the room was dated but otherwise in good condition. The only remaining evidence to be called relates to the type and extent of the damages. 48 The Rule 7.1(a) test set out in Gallant is “a real likelihood that the net result will save time and money for all concerned”. Based on the facts before me, I find there is a real likelihood that proceeding with summary judgment on liability will save time and costs. The criteria set out in Rule 7.1(a) are met. I am satisfied that this has been a fair and just process and there is no issue of merit with respect to liability that requires a trial. A finding of liability on these facts is fair and just to all parties. I am also satisfied that it is advantageous to the proceedings as a whole to grant summary judgement on the issue of liability and direct the parties to continue with an assessment of damages. This approach is consistent with the Foundational Rules and the approach in Hyrniak. 7. Summary Judgment Against One of Several Defendants In Ratch v. Macleod, 2011 ABQB 820, 2011 CarswellAlta 2314, Justice Graesser said, at paragraph 24: 24 Rule 7.2 dealing with summary judgment provides that a party can apply for summary judgment at any time. There is no impediment to a plaintiff seeking summary judgment, or an assessment of damages, against one defendant, leaving claims against another defendant unresolved. Indeed, when one of two or more defendants has been noted in default, a plaintiff may well want to proceed swiftly against the party in default and litigate against the defending party later (if at all). 8. Judgment Based on Admissions The substantive principles applicable to rule 162 are the same as those applicable to rule 159: 365733 Alberta Ltd. v. 794608 Alberta Ltd. (September 6, 2001), Calgary 0001 19504 (Alta. Q.B.). Furthermore, there is no bar to judgment under rule 162 if the admissions made by the defendant entitle the plaintiff to the relief sought in a Statement of Claim: Zama Holdings Ltd. v. Metropolitan Trust Co. of Canada (1996), 43 Alta. L.R. (3d) 156 (Q.B.). As was found in 365733, supra and Jager Industries Inc. v. Canadian Occidental Petroleum Ltd. et al. (2000), 273 A.R. 1, 84 Alta. L.R. (3d) 353 (Q.B.), at pp. 363-365 [Alta. L.R.], the following factors are relevant in the determination of such an application: (a) where a Respondent to a summary judgment application has made admissions which establish the Appellant's cause of action or defence, the burden of proof shifts to the Respondent, who must then adduce some evidence, as opposed to mere allegations, to establish a triable issue; (b) it is not open to a Respondent on a summary judgment application to argue that a triable issue exists based upon facts or evidence not currently available but which “may” emerge at discovery or trial; (c) where an Applicant has shown there are no facts in issue for trial, it is incumbent upon the Respondent to adduce evidence that it has a reasonable chance of success at trial; (d) it is insufficient for a Respondent who resists summary judgment to present only bare allegations of fact; the Respondent must present evidence which lends some support to the claims it advances; and (e) a summary judgment application may be made at any time. Summary judgment cannot be given if there are difficult or intricate legal issues, or if the evidence conflicts. The admissions relied upon must be clear and unambiguous. The purpose of the rule is to permit the Court to dispose of defences that have no merit on the basis of admissions made in the pleadings, in the documents, or on discovery. Simply put, a trial is unnecessary where it is clear from the defendant's admissions that the plaintiff will succeed at trial. 732311 Alberta Ltd. v. Paradise Bay Spa & Tub Warehouse Inc. ((2003),), 15 Alta. L.R. (4th) 42 ((Q.B.)) at 54-55, per Johnstone J. 9. Admissions by Notice to Admit Rule 6.37 permits a party to serve a notice requiring a party to admit certain facts set out in the notice. A deemed admission is made if a proper response is not made. Those deemed admissions can form the basis of a R. 162 application—even if the other party is an infant. … the facts alleged in the Notice to Admit Facts must be taken to be binding on the infant plaintiff. Millard v. Millard (1983), 65 A.R. 355 at 357 C.A. 10. Informal Admissions In Gerling Global General Insurance Co. v. Canadian Occidental Petroleum Ltd. (1998), 64 Alta. L.R. (3d) 174 (Q.B.); [additional reasons (1998) 64 Alta. L.R. (3d) 196 (Q.B.)], Madam Justice Romaine discussed informal admissions and when they can bind the party making them. She specifically considered informal admissions as the basis for an application for judgment. In her judgment, Her Ladyship refered to several other judgments and can be taken to have approved the propositions for which they stand. At pp. 182-85, Romaine J. said: Rule 162(a) of the Alberta Rules of Court provides that, at any stage of the proceedings, the court may, upon application, give any judgment or order to which the applicant may be entitled when admissions of fact have been made on the pleadings or otherwise. The issue here is whether the evidence proffered by the Insurers would fall within the meaning of or “otherwise”. The admissions put forward are not formal admissions, but they may constitute informal admissions as statements made outside the litigation process in Alberta. While formal admissions are binding on the party that made them unless the court gives leave to withdraw them, the general view is that informal admissions are prima facie admissible, but that they may or may not be binding on the party that made them, depending on the circumstances under which they were made. A party may adduce evidence to contradict or explain an informal admission (Schiff, Evidence in the Litigation Process, 4th ed. at 442-445). In R. v. Dipietro (1993), 108 D.L.R. (4th) 32 (S.C.C.), the Supreme Court of Canada held that the rationale for admitting admissions has a different basis than other exceptions to the hearsay rule, and that it may in fact be disputed whether admission evidence is hearsay at all. Sopinka, J. said at page 39 of the decision that the admissibility of admissions “rests on the theory of the adversary system that what a party has previously stated can be admitted against the party in whose mouth it does not lie to complain of the unreliability of his or her own statements”. The Supreme Court confirmed that the rule is the same for both criminal and civil cases. As exceptions to the hearsay rule, informal admissions are admissible to prove the truth of the matter admitted. Rule 162 differs from Rule 159 in that there is no requirement in Rule 162 that the evidence come from someone who can swear directly to the facts. This makes sense, because Rule 162 contemplates admissions that are not in affidavit form (Wigmore on Evidence, Chadbourn Revision, 4th (1972), at para. 1048). In what circumstances should informal admissions be relied upon for judgment? In Canadian Mine Enterprises Ltd. v. Scottie Gold Mines Ltd. (1982), 30 C.P.C. 47 (B.C. S.C.), the plaintiff claimed for a sum owing for services rendered pursuant to a contract. The plaintiff argued that, in correspondence received from the defendant prior to the commencement of the action, the defendant admitted that the sum was owing. The plaintiff sought judgment on the basis of these admissions. The Court declined to grant judgment in that case, stating that for a court to grant judgment on admissions, the admission must be made in circumstances surrounded with sufficient formality that the defendant would weigh his words with care, recognizing that they would be looked at carefully and that he will be bound by them. The case of Phil Whittaker Logging Ltd. v. British Columbia Hydro & Power Authority (1985), 5 C.P.C. (2d) 71 (B.C. S.C.) involved an application for summary judgment. Shortly after the action commenced, the defendant's first solicitor admitted liability to the plaintiff by way of a telephone conversation and subsequently by correspondence. Two years later the defendant's new solicitor tried to withdraw the admission. The plaintiff opposed the withdrawal and brought an application for judgment based on the admission. The issues before the Court was whether the admission of liability was a proper admission for the purposes of the British Columbia equivalent of Rule 162. The Court held that, although the admission was not a judicial or formal one in the form of a Statement of Defence or a Notice to Admit Facts, it was an admission upon which judgment could be based. A non-judicial admission is binding as long as the Court does not grant leave for its withdrawal. The informal admission could only be withdrawn if, in the circumstances, the Court is satisfied that it is in the interest of justice to do so. The factors that should be considered when determining whether the admission is binding are: i) whether the admission was made inadvertently or hastily; ii) whether it was made with knowledge of the facts; or iii) whether new facts have come to light since the admission was made. Whittaker was overturned in McLuskie v. Sakai, [1987] 4 W.W.R. 609 (B.C. C.A.). McLuskie is distinguishable on the basis that the British Columbia rule concerning judgment on admission is inextricably linked to a Notice to Admit Facts. Outside of the procedural impediment, the Court of Appeal's [sic] reasoning in Whittaker is consistent with that in other courts. The Court's concern is that an admission must be made in a sufficiently formal manner to ensure that the party making the admission has considered its words carefully. Statements made by a party's representative in his or her capacity as such may be binding as admissions against the party if the relationship between the parties gives rise to a sufficient privity or identity of interest. This would include any relationship which permits one person's rights, obligations or remedies to be affected by the acts of another person and if the representative has been authorized to make the statement. (J. Sopinka, The Law of Evidence in Canada at 289-294). In Caviglia v. Tenorio (1992), 71 B.C.L.R. (2d) 255 (B.C. S.C.), followed in Theriault v. Patrick (March 22, 1995), Doc. Vancouver B931678 (B.C. Master), an admission made in another action before the same court was accepted as admissible. The plaintiff was the driver of a car which slid off the road after hitting a patch of ice. The defendant was the driver of another car which hit the same patch of ice and slid into the plaintiff's car (the “first action”). A second action was brought by the passenger in the defendant's vehicle. The defendant's insurer assumed conduct of both actions. The defendant denied liability in the first action but admitted liability in the second action. The plaintiff in the first action brought an application for summary judgment. The Court in Caviglia held that an admission made in separate proceedings was admissible, but not conclusive. The weight to be given to the admission is to be determined in the particular circumstances in which it was made. . . . . . If an admission is admissible and given in circumstances suggesting that great weight should be placed on it, the next step is to determine whether judgment should be granted. 11. Withdrawal of Informal Admissions An informal admission may only be withdrawn if the court is satisfied that in the circumstances, it is in the interests of justice to do so. The concern is that the admission must have been made in a manner to ensure the party making the admission had considered his or her words carefully. The factors which should be considered to determine whether it is in the interest of justice to withdraw the admission were described by the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Norlympia Seafoods Ltd. v. Dale and Co. (1982), 141 D.L.R. (3d) 733 (B.C. C.A.), at p. 737: “(i) whether an admission was made inadvertently or hastily; (ii) whether it was made with knowledge of the facts; or (iii) whether new facts have come to light since the admission was made.”Becker v. Director of Employment Standards (Alta.) et al. (2000), 277 A.R. 131 (C.A.) at 134-135, per curiam. 12. Single Action Not Severable One may not divide up a single action. If the plaintiff alleges one debt, the defendant's admission that part of the debt is owing does not permit an application under R. 162 for judgment for the admitted amount and a direction that the action proceed in respect of the disputed amount. After a review of the authorities and consideration of RR. 159-164 of the Alberta Rules of Court, I am satisfied that our rules do not permit the granting of summary judgment for part of a claim when the dispute is the amount due and owing in a simple debt action. There is but one claim in this action, the debt, and the amount due and owing is not severable from the debt. It is the very issue to be tried. The plaintiffs in this case seek judgment upon the pleadings. By so doing, they have not joined issue with the defendants. They have accepted the statement of defence and the position of the corporate defendant on the affidavit filed in answer to the motion. By accepting the defendants' pleadings and affidavit, they must accept the negative as well as the affirmative allegations set forth therein for the purposes of this motion … The plaintiffs are therefore not entitled to judgment upon the motion with leave to proceed on the action for the balance for their claim in debt. The admission of the corporate defendant is not sufficient to enable the plaintiffs to recover partial judgment and at the same time retain the right to proceed against the corporate defendant for the disputed amount. Great West Imports Ltd. v. Harmony Lane Music Studios & Instrument Sales Ltd. (1986), 45 Alta. L.R. (2d) 340 342-43 (Q.B.). 13. No Disputed Facts And it is very well established that judgment can be given under R. 162 only if the admissions are clear and unequivocal. This Rule is no more suitable for determining contested facts or weighing facts, than is summary judgment under R. 159. Zickefoose (Next friend of) v. Barotto Sports Ltd. (1992), 7 Alta. L.R. (3d) 359 at 361 (C.A.). And Master Funduk has said: The guiding hand to a rule 162 application is Zickefoose v. Barotto Sports Ltd.… The rule is not suitable for determining contested facts or weighing facts. Hill v. Richert (1996), 180 A.R. 156 at 159 (Master). 14. Admissions as the Basis for Summary Judgment In Admiral Canada Inc. v. Freekick Ltd., 2006 ABQB 451, 2006 CarswellAlta 1761, 406 A.R. 91, 67 Alta. L.R. (4th) 376, Moen J. said, at p. 378: 8 Rule 162 of the Alberta Rules of Court permits the Court to grant any judgment or order to which an applicant may be entitled when admissions of fact have been made on the pleadings or otherwise. In this case the Plaintiff alleges that admissions were made in correspondence and in the Examination for Discovery of the Defendants. 9 The Alberta Court of Appeal has said that Summary Judgment under Rule 162 may be granted where admissions are clear and unequivocal: Zickefoose (Next Friend of) v. Barotto Sports Ltd. (1992), 131 A.R. 292 at 294 (C.A.); Shell Canada Resources Limited v. Ralph M. Parsons Company of Canada Ltd., [1981] 4 W.W.R. 647 (Q.B.); Majestic Mines Ltd. v. Royal Trust Co., [1930] 1 W.W.R. 106 (Alta. S.C.A.D). Moen J. then defined the term “admissions” (at pp. 378-379): 14 “‘Admissions’ are concessions or voluntary acknowledgements made by a party of the existence of certain facts. More accurately regarded, they are statements by a party, or some one identified with him in his legal interest, of the existence of a fact which is relevant to the cause of his adversary …”: Vector Energy Inc. v. Canadian Pioneer Energy Inc. (1996), 185 A.R. 214 (Q.B. Master) at 217. 15. Third Parties A court may not strike a third party notice on the ground that the defendant is bound to succeed against the plaintiff. A court should not strike third party proceedings on the grouind that the defendant must and will succeed in a defence. That decision should be made in a motion that will bind the plaintiff. Third party proceedings are always conditional on the plaintiff proving its case. Counsel expressed great frustration about this. They said they had no way, as third parties, to strike at the plaintiffs to end their involvement in litigation they consider to be frivolous and abusive. Counsel for the defendants responded that they had decided to delay motions to dismiss the cliam summarily until after the completion of examinations for discovery. Other than to seek security for costs, it may well be that the third parties must wait. Allied-Signal Inc. v. Dome Petroleum Ltd. (1992), 3 Alta. L.R. (3d) 155 at 157-58 (C.A.).
